I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette: Malik was nineteen when the attention stopped feeling like a fleeting crush and began feeling like a trap. It started with a classmate from his first semester, someone he had only spoken to twice in passing. Within weeks, he noticed his social media feeds were being manipulated, his location tags appearing on accounts he hadn’t used, and a familiar sedan idling outside his apartment complex. The escalation crystallized in October. He was walking back to the library after a late shift when he saw the same man standing under a streetlamp, watching him approach. The next day, a package arrived with no return address, containing a printed screenshot of Malik’s own public profile, circled in red. By the time the police filed a restraining order, the man had moved on, leaving behind a residue of fear rather than a clear resolution. In the months that followed, Malik found himself recalibrating his entire environment. At his new role as a junior UX designer, he sat in an open-plan studio where glass walls and shared monitors were meant to foster collaboration. Instead, the glowing screens became sources of tension. Whenever a notification chimed or a colleague leaned over his desk to review a wireframe, his pulse would spike. He began logging into his work computer only after checking the surrounding rooms, running his fingers along the edges of his monitor to ensure nothing was hidden. He switched to incognito browsers, changed every password twice a month, and deleted his old location-sharing apps, convinced that any piece of digital footfall could be weaponized. He had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. Crosswalks felt exposed; he took the longer route to the subway, timing his steps to the rhythm of passing cars. He had come to believe the world was a dangerous place, a place where harm could materialize from a misplaced glance or an unsecured account. Alongside this hyperawareness, a persistent guilt took root. Malik replayed his interactions with the stalker in his mind, convinced he had misread signals, sent the wrong email, or failed to set boundaries early enough. The event happened because of the way I acted, he told himself whenever he caught a stranger staring at his phone. He stopped attending department mixers, declined weekend studio critiques, and began working remotely for weeks at a time, telling his supervisor he was deep in user-testing cycles. He pulled away from his girlfriend, unable to tolerate the casual intimacy of shared plans or the vulnerability of letting someone else know his schedule. The avoidance solidified into habit, narrowing his days into a quiet loop of checking locks, deleting metadata, and avoiding eye contact in crowded breaks. Now, at the end of his first year in the role, Malik is sitting in a therapist’s office for the first time. He still checks the lock on his apartment door three times, and he still flinches when a stranger’s eyes linger on his phone screen. But what finally brought him through the clinic’s revolving doors was a Tuesday morning when he stared at a design prototype for forty minutes, paralyzed by the fear that someone was watching the progress, and realized he was losing the part of himself that used to enjoy creating things. He is hoping to untangle the guilt from the reality of what happened, and he is terrified that no amount of caution will ever be enough to keep the world from closing in again.
